title: Hukuru Miskiy (Old Friday Mosque)
summary: A UNESCO-listed 17th-century coral-stone mosque in Malé, famed for its intricate carvings and lacquer work.
body: Male Friday Mosque, also known as Hukuru Miskiy, is one of the oldest and most significant mosques in the Maldives. Built in 1658, it is renowned for its intricate coral stone architecture, traditional wood carvings and lacquer work, and is a UNESCO World Heritage tentative site. Visitors can explore the mosque's ancient inscriptions, tombstones and architectural features to learn about the history and cultural heritage of the Maldives. The mosque is still active, so dress modestly and respect local customs while visiting.

title: The National Museum
summary: The Maldives' National Museum, housed in a former royal palace in Sultan Park, Malé.
body: The National Museum of Maldives is located in Sultan Park, housed in a former royal palace. The museum showcases the rich history and culture of the Maldives, with exhibits ranging from ancient artifacts and royal regalia to traditional costumes and weapons. Visitors can learn about the Maldives' history, from its Buddhist period to the Islamic era, through the museum's extensive collection — an excellent stop for families and history buffs.

title: Mulee'aage (The President's Palace)
summary: The official residence of the President of the Maldives, an early-20th-century colonial-style palace in Malé.
body: Mulee'aage, the official residence of the President of the Maldives, is a striking example of colonial architecture in Malé. Built in the early 20th century, the palace is known for its elaborate carvings, vibrant colors and well-manicured gardens. Visitors aren't allowed inside, but the exterior offers a great photography spot and a popular stop on walking tours of Malé.
best_for: A quick photo stop on a Malé walking tour

title: Sultan Park and Rasrani Bageecha
summary: A lush green park in the heart of Malé, once part of the royal palace grounds and home to the National Museum.
body: Sultan Park, also known as Rasrani Bageecha, is a lush green space in the heart of Malé, offering a peaceful retreat from the city's hustle and bustle. The park was once part of the royal palace grounds and now features well-maintained gardens, playgrounds and water features. It's an ideal spot for families to relax, with plenty of shaded areas, benches and play areas for children, and is also home to the National Museum — a convenient stop for those exploring Malé's cultural sites.
best_for: Families wanting a relaxed break in central Malé

title: Maldives Islamic Centre
summary: A prominent Malé landmark topped by a large golden dome, home to the largest mosque in the Maldives.
body: The Maldives Islamic Centre is one of the most prominent landmarks in Malé. The centre is known for its large golden dome, which dominates the city's skyline. The mosque inside is the largest in the Maldives and can accommodate over 5,000 worshippers. Visitors are welcome to explore the mosque outside of prayer times, providing an opportunity to learn about Islamic architecture and culture in the Maldives — the centre also hosts cultural events and exhibitions throughout the year.
best_for: Learning about Islamic architecture and culture

title: Artificial Beach
summary: A popular man-made beach on the eastern side of Malé, used for swimming, water sports and community events.
body: Artificial Beach is a man-made beach located on the eastern side of Malé. It's a popular spot for locals and tourists alike, offering a place to swim, relax and enjoy the sunset, and is a hub for various water sports and beach activities. The beach often hosts community events, including music festivals, parades and carnivals — a great place to experience local culture and enjoy some leisure time by the sea.
best_for: Swimming, sunset views, and local community events

title: Victory Monument
summary: A Malé monument near Republic Square commemorating the government's victory over a 1988 coup attempt.
body: The Victory Monument in Malé commemorates the victory of the Maldives government over a coup attempt in 1988. The monument is located near Republic Square and serves as a reminder of the country's modern political history. It's worth a quick visit for those interested in that history, and is located in a central area that's easy to include in a walking tour of Malé.
best_for: A quick stop on a Malé walking tour

title: Tsunami Monument
summary: A memorial on the southeastern side of Malé commemorating the lives lost in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
body: The Tsunami Monument, located on the southeastern part of Malé, commemorates the lives lost in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. The monument features a design with spheres representing the victims and steel rods symbolizing the impact of the waves. Visitors can reflect on the tragedy and resilience of the Maldivian people, with the surrounding area offering a peaceful environment with ocean views.
best_for: A quiet, reflective stop with ocean views

title: Malé Fish Market
summary: A bustling working fish market in Malé where locals buy and sell the day's catch, famous for feeding the resident stingrays.
body: The Fish Market in Malé is a vibrant, bustling place where locals buy and sell fresh seafood — an excellent spot to witness the daily life of Malé's residents and experience local food culture. Visitors can observe fishermen bringing in their catch of the day and even buy fresh fish to be cooked at nearby restaurants. The fishermen's jetty in front of the market is where fish waste is discarded, a daily practice that draws stingrays which visitors can watch or feed.
best_for: Experiencing everyday local life and culture

title: Republic Square (Jumhooree Maidhaan)
summary: Malé's central public square, surrounded by government buildings and the site of national celebrations.
body: Republic Square, also known as Jumhooree Maidhaan, is a central square in Malé that serves as a popular gathering place for locals. The square is surrounded by important government buildings, including the Presidential Palace and the headquarters of the Maldivian National Defence Force. It's often the site of national celebrations, parades and other public events — a great place to observe local culture and the city's atmosphere.
best_for: Observing local culture and public events

title: Sinamalé Bridge
summary: The China-Maldives Friendship Bridge connecting Malé to Hulhulé Island and Velana International Airport.
body: The Sinamalé Bridge, also known as the China-Maldives Friendship Bridge, connects Malé with Hulhulé Island, where Velana International Airport is located. The bridge is a significant engineering achievement that has improved transportation between the islands. Visitors can walk or drive across it to enjoy panoramic views of the Indian Ocean and surrounding islands — it's particularly beautiful at sunset, making it a popular photography spot.

title: Rasfannu Beach
summary: A small, popular urban beach on the western side of Malé, well known as a spot to watch the sunset.
body: Rasfannu Beach is a small but popular urban beach located on the western side of Malé. The beach offers a convenient spot for swimming, sunbathing and relaxing, with facilities such as showers, changing rooms and food stalls nearby. It's a great place to catch the sunset in Malé, well-maintained and with a laid-back atmosphere that makes it a favorite for both locals and tourists.
best_for: Sunset views and a relaxed local beach atmosphere
